subject: AI & Agents
title: k-Nearest Neighbors: You Are Who You're Near
description: A micro-lesson that makes k-Nearest Neighbors: You Are Who You're Near usable.

hook.text: To classify a new data point, just look at its closest neighbors and go with the majority.

buildup.text: k-NN stores all training data and classifies new points by proximity.

discovery.text: If three of your five nearest neighbors are cats, you're probably a cat too.

twist.text: It struggles in high dimensions — the 'curse of dimensionality' makes distances meaningless.

climax.text: Despite its simplicity, k-NN works surprisingly well for recommendation systems.

punchline.text: The simplest algorithm: ask your neighbors.

quiz.question: How does k-Nearest Neighbors classify a new data point?
options: By majority vote of the closest training examples

details.summary: K-nearest neighbors classifies new data points by looking at the labels of their closest neighbors in the training data. If most nearby points are cats, the new point is probably a cat too.
details.whyItMatters: KNN demonstrates the simplest form of machine learning — learning by analogy. Its intuitive logic makes it a great entry point for understanding how AI uses similarity to make predictions.
takeaways: KNN classifies based on the labels of the closest training points
It requires no training phase — predictions use the raw data
Simple and intuitive but slow for large datasets

faq.question: What does the 'k' in KNN represent?
faq.answer: k is the number of neighbors consulted. With k=3, the algorithm checks the 3 closest training points and takes a majority vote. Choosing k involves a tradeoff between noise sensitivity and smoothness.

faq.question: Why is KNN called a lazy learner?
faq.answer: It does no computation during training — it simply stores the data. All work happens at prediction time when it searches for nearest neighbors. This makes training instant but prediction slow for large datasets.
